demographics.narrative:
Australia's population was 27.9 million at 31 March 2026, up 392,700 on a year earlier, a growth rate of 1.4 percent.{{3}} Net overseas migration added 292,100 people over the year and natural increase added 100,600.{{3}} Western Australia grew fastest at 2.1 percent and Tasmania slowest at 0.6 percent.{{3}} In the 2021 Census, 27.6 percent of residents were born overseas, and the most common languages used at home other than English were Mandarin, Arabic, Vietnamese, Cantonese and Punjabi.{{11}} About 88 percent of people live in urban areas on the United Nations definition the World Bank uses, and about 68 percent live in the eight capital cities.{{7}}{{4}}{{5}}

The population is aging. People aged 65 and over made up 17.7 percent of residents at 31 March 2026, the median age was 38.4 years in mid-2025, and the fertility rate was 1.497 births per woman in 2025.{{4}}{{6}}{{8}} Life expectancy at birth in 2022 to 2024 was 81.1 years for males and 85.1 years for females, unchanged from 2021 to 2023, and the OECD puts the overall figure at 83 years, 1.9 years above its average.{{9}}{{10}} For a foreign academic medical center, this points to steady demand for care of chronic and age-related conditions in a high-income, mostly insured population served largely by the domestic system.

disease_prevalence.narrative:
Dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, was Australia's leading cause of death again in 2025, with 19,019 of the 188,421 registered deaths, or 10.1 percent, the first year above 10 percent.{{1}} Ischemic heart diseases were second at 8.6 percent, and their age-standardized death rate was the lowest on record, down from a peak in 1968.{{1}} Dementia deaths rose 37.3 percent between 2016 and 2025 while ischemic heart disease deaths fell 16.2 percent.{{1}}

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare estimates about 170,000 new cancer cases in 2025, and five-year relative survival has risen from 50 percent to 72 percent since 1987 to 1991.{{5}} The latest national health survey, from 2022, found 65.8 percent of adults overweight or obese, 10.6 percent smoking daily (down from 22.4 percent in 2001), 4.0 percent currently vaping and 5.3 percent with diabetes, and half of the population had a chronic condition.{{4}}{{3}}{{2}} The burden points to sustained demand in cardiovascular care, oncology, neurology, diabetes care and aged care.

private_system.narrative:
Private health insurance sits beside Medicare. At 30 June 2026, 12,823,752 people (45.8 percent of the population) held hospital cover, and insurers paid A$5.33 billion (US$3.74 billion) in hospital benefits in the June quarter.{{1}} Under community rating, insurers cannot price by health status, and risk equalization shares the claims of members aged 55 and over, and very high claims, across all insurers.{{10}}{{11}} Hospital policies come in four tiers, and members are moving down: Gold fell from 40.1 percent of hospital policies in December 2020 to 29.3 percent in December 2025.{{2}}

Government encourages cover with a premium rebate, the Medicare levy surcharge and Lifetime Health Cover loading.{{4}}{{6}}{{7}} The 2026-27 Budget removes the rebate's age-based uplift from 1 April 2027, saving A$3.0 billion (US$2.1 billion) over four years for aged care.{{5}} Premiums rose 4.41 percent on average on 1 April 2026.{{3}} Legislation passed in September 2026 requires ministerial approval of premiums on new products, bars closing and reopening a product at a higher price, and lets the government publish individual specialists' fees.{{12}}

financing.narrative:
Total health spending was A$290.7 billion (US$204 billion) in 2024-25, or A$10,614 (US$7,440) per person and 10.5 percent of GDP, up 3.4 percent in real terms, and governments funded 70 percent of it.{{1}}{{2}} Hospitals took A$123.4 billion (US$86.5 billion) and primary health care A$93.0 billion (US$65.2 billion).{{2}}

The OECD's series counts current expenditure only, so its shares differ from the AIHW's. It puts spending at 10.84 percent of GDP in 2024 and 11.15 percent in 2025, both OECD estimates, above the unweighted OECD means of 9.30 and 9.36 percent.{{3}} At purchasing power parity, spending per person was US$7,885 in 2024, against a mean of US$6,100.{{4}} Government schemes paid 72.7 percent, below the mean of 75.2 percent, and households paid 15.7 percent out of pocket in 2023, against 19.5 percent.{{5}}{{6}} The Commonwealth budgets A$136.9 billion (US$96 billion) for health in 2026-27.{{7}}

workforce.narrative:
On the OECD's measure of practising physicians, Australia had 4.29 per 1,000 people in 2024, above the unweighted mean of 4.02 across 33 members. The licensed-to-practice measure gives 5.22 against a mean of 5.71, so the comparison depends on which group is counted.{{1}} Nurses are well above the mean at 13.42 per 1,000 against 9.93, and CT scanners number 75.4 per million people against 28.8, while MRI units are below the mean.{{2}}{{3}}

The medical register held 153,963 practitioners in 2025/26, up 3.9 percent, and 6,098 of the 10,248 first-time registrants trained overseas.{{4}} The Expedited Specialist pathway, opened in 2024 for specialists from comparable systems, has drawn 942 applications, 807 of them from GPs.{{4}} Distribution is uneven: four in five specialists registered in the pathway's first six months work in major cities, according to Medical Republic.{{5}}

competitive_landscape.narrative: Twenty-two foreign partnerships with Australian institutions are active, each confirmed by dated evidence since October 2024. Most are university research and training links, such as Emory University with the University of Queensland and Ochsner Health's joint MD program with Queensland.{{1}}{{2}} Northern Sydney Local Health District runs a cancer clinical trials facility at Royal North Shore Hospital whose investigators partner with Memorial Sloan Kettering on international trials, and Mayo Clinic advises TLC Healthcare on a new day surgery hospital in Victoria.{{3}}{{4}}
competitive_landscape.closing: Australia sends more patients out than it takes in. An undated Victorian Government estimate puts the number of Australians traveling abroad for care at about 15,000 a year, mostly for cosmetic and dental work in Asia, and the federal Medical Treatment Overseas Program funds a small number of life-threatening cases, notably proton therapy in the United States.{{5}}{{6}}{{7}} Inbound flows are small and regional: visitors and students who carry insurance, and Papua New Guinea residents treated at Torres Strait clinics.{{8}}{{9}}

facts.label: Medical Treatment Overseas Program (MTOP)
facts.value: Federal program that gives financial help to Australian residents with a life-threatening or life-limiting condition to be treated overseas when an effective alternative is not available in Australia{{1}}

facts.label: What MTOP pays
facts.value: Treatment, accommodation and airfares for the patient and one support person, as described in a 2024 interview study; the program books the flights{{1}}

facts.label: How a case reaches MTOP
facts.value: A treating radiation oncologist can suggest an application; for proton therapy the Royal Adelaide Hospital has run a photon versus proton comparison planning service since 2016 to accompany applications{{1}}

facts.label: Case numbers
facts.value: No annual total found on a page we could open. In an unstated two-year period the Royal Adelaide Hospital's planning service handled 43 referrals and 19 MTOP applications, and 16 approved patients traveled{{1}}

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: Median 7 weeks from application to approval (range 4 to 16) among seven families who traveled 2017 to 2020; travel followed 1 to 4 weeks after approval{{1}}

facts.label: Destinations
facts.value: Five of the seven families interviewed were treated in US centers and two in European centers{{1}}

facts.label: 2026 federal position
facts.value: In August 2026 the health minister said the program funds young patients, usually children, to go overseas, usually to the United States, and that some barriers to access for families had been lifted{{2}}

facts.label: Proton therapy in Australia
facts.value: No operating proton therapy facility as of February 2026{{3}}

facts.label: Adelaide (Australian Bragg Centre)
facts.value: SAHMRI announced a delay in February 2024 over supply chain problems{{4}}; treatment was once expected by 2025, and in February 2026 SAHMRI won A$35 million (US$24.5 million) in damages from the supplier, ProTom International{{3}}

facts.label: Melbourne
facts.value: Victoria committed A$50 million (US$35.1 million) in 2016 toward a national center in Parkville to be run by Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre{{5}}; the Commonwealth is reviewing the Victorian proposal{{2}}

facts.label: Federal decision
facts.value: On 21 August 2026 the minister said Cancer Australia advice points to demand for more than one unit, possibly Adelaide and Melbourne, and that a Commonwealth budget decision is still needed{{2}}

facts.label: Sydney
facts.value: ANSTO and hospital and university partners propose a National Particle Treatment and Research Centre centered on carbon ion therapy; ANSTO's page presents it as a proposal and lists the Westmead precinct among stakeholders{{6}}

facts.label: Volume of medical tourism
facts.value: An undated estimate from Victoria's Better Health Channel is about 15,000 Australians traveling overseas for health care each year; cosmetic surgery tourism alone is put at about A$300 million (US$210 million) a year{{7}}

facts.label: Where and why
facts.value: Mostly Thailand, India, South Korea, Turkey and Malaysia for cheaper cosmetic and dental care, with spinal, hip, knee, shoulder and fertility care becoming more common; savings can reach 80 percent{{7}}

facts.label: Dental
facts.value: Dental care is not subsidized for most Australians and, in 2018, about half had no private dental cover; popular destinations are Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines{{8}}

facts.label: Warnings
facts.value: The Australian Medical Association and the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons warn against overseas surgery{{7}}

facts.label: Visitors and Medicare
facts.value: Most overseas visitors are not eligible for Medicare and pay the full cost of public hospital care; reciprocal agreements cover essential treatment only{{9}}

facts.label: Reciprocal agreement countries
facts.value: United Kingdom, Sweden, Netherlands, Belgium, Slovenia, Italy, New Zealand, Norway, Finland, Malta and Ireland (students from Norway, Finland, Malta and Ireland are not covered by the agreements){{19}}

facts.label: International students
facts.value: Overseas Student Health Cover is a condition of a student visa; it covers hospital and medical care and ambulance, with limited pharmaceutical benefits{{10}}

facts.label: Inbound medical tourism count
facts.value: No official figure found on a page we could open

facts.label: Torres Strait and Papua New Guinea
facts.value: A 2011 review found PNG residents regularly crossed to Queensland Health clinics on Saibai and Boigu islands, with acute life-threatening cases evacuated to Thursday Island Hospital or the mainland{{11}}

facts.label: Pacific referrals
facts.value: New Zealand's Pacific scheme accepts referrals for treatment in New Zealand, Australia or Fiji{{12}}; overseas medical referral is common across 16 Pacific island countries{{13}}

facts.label: US-trained doctors
facts.value: The Medical Board lists the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates (US) among the competent authorities whose assessed doctors can register through the Competent Authority pathway; no count of US-trained doctors in Australia found{{14}}

facts.label: UQ-Ochsner MD program
facts.value: Two years in Brisbane and two in New Orleans; 82 graduates in 2025 and more than 1,000 alumni; 95 percent match rate for the Class of 2025{{15}}{{16}}

facts.label: American Australian Association exchange
facts.value: US$40,000 per clinician to work three months or more at St Vincent's Hospital Sydney or at a US institution; first fields are movement disorders, pain management and nursing in cellular therapies{{17}}

facts.label: Epworth and Cleveland Clinic
facts.value: Two-year colorectal fellowship: year 1 at Epworth Richmond, year 2 at Cleveland Clinic; the 2026 intake starts February 2026{{18}}

recent_developments.headline: GP bulk billing was 83.6 percent in July to September 2026
recent_developments.summary: Government figures show 83.6 percent of GP services were bulk billed in July to September 2026, up from 77.6 percent a year earlier and down slightly from 84.1 percent in April to June. More than 4,000 practices now bill every patient without a fee, and the rate was 93.2 percent for concession card holders and 75.4 percent for other patients.{{1}}

sources.author: Mark Butler
sources.title: Bulk billing continues to increase year on year

recent_developments.headline: Dementia passes 10 percent of deaths in ABS 2025 data
recent_developments.summary: ABS figures show dementia caused 19,019 of 188,421 registered deaths in 2025, or 10.1 percent, the first year above 10 percent. Ischemic heart diseases were second at 8.6 percent, and their age-standardized death rate was the lowest on record, down from a peak in 1968.{{1}}

sources.author: Australian Bureau of Statistics
sources.title: Causes of Death, Australia, 2025

recent_developments.headline: Healthscope's 25 remaining hospitals to be divided among four operators
recent_developments.summary: Receivers announced that 25 Healthscope hospitals and its central services platform will go to Calvary Health Care (14 hospitals), Healthe Care (6), ACURIO Health (3) and KnG Group (2), with completion targeted for 30 November 2026, subject to regulatory approvals.{{1}}{{2}} Healthscope entered receivership in May 2025 after its owner Brookfield withdrew support.{{2}} In mid-November Calvary said the 30 November handover of its 14 hospitals would be delayed, and the ACCC has not yet decided on the sale.{{3}}

recent_developments.headline: 2026-27 Budget funds hospitals, urgent care and a private insurance rebate change
recent_developments.summary: The Budget gives the states A$220.3 billion (US$154 billion) over five years for public hospitals and the funding addendum, and A$1.8 billion (US$1.26 billion) over five years from 2025-26 for Medicare Urgent Care Clinics. It removes the age-based uplift of the private health insurance rebate from 1 April 2027, saving A$3.0 billion (US$2.1 billion) over four years.{{1}}

sources.title: Budget Measures 2026-27 (Budget Paper No. 2)

recent_developments.headline: National Cabinet agrees new public hospital funding deal
recent_developments.summary: National Cabinet agreed A$25 billion (US$17.5 billion) in additional Commonwealth funding for public hospitals, which the Prime Minister said is three times the increase under the last five-year agreement.{{1}} The addendum to the National Health Reform Agreement covers 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2031.{{1}}{{2}}

resolution_log: Disease prevalence: ischemic heart disease wording corrected to match the ABS ('lowest on record, down from a 1968 peak'); cancer figures now cite the AIHW overview. The AIHW 2025 National Drug Strategy Household Survey smoking rate (5.6 percent of people 14 and over) could not be confirmed here and is not included; the 2022 ABS figure keeps its year.

Public system: Medicare safety net thresholds updated to the 2026 calendar year; bulk billing cited to the Minister's 17 November 2026 release with the April to June 2026 rate (84.1 percent) for context; dollar equivalents recomputed; contribution rate and price sources tightened.
Private system: Medicare levy surcharge thresholds updated from 2024-25 to 2026-27; insurer shares labeled as CHOICE's summary of APRA data.

Hospitals: Healthscope sale described as announced in September 2026 with the November delay and ACCC position; completed and pending earlier sales separated; Ramsay counted as 44 facilities; private sector loss attributed to APHA citing ABS and the insurer comparison removed because it is disputed; private beds statement corrected. The AIHW 2024-25 public hospital counts could not be read, so the 2023-24 figures keep their year labels.

Financing: OECD 2024 and 2025 values labeled as estimates (the OECD flags both as estimated) in the facts, text and 1 chart notes; headline spending figures now cite AIHW Health expenditure Australia 2024-25.
Outlook: contribution rate stated as a schedule; dementia claim now cites the ABS 2025 causes of death release; Calvary delay updated.

Patient flows: MTOP rules attributed to the 2024 interview study they rest on (the Department's page was unreadable); medical tourism volume labeled as an undated Victorian estimate; dental statistic dated 2018; reciprocal agreements now cite Services Australia with the student caveat.
